k6aud/_final_k7t1|s-l1-back-to-school: It is the first of September. The school yard is full of flowers, balloons and noisy students. Taras and Marichka are in the seventh form now, and they are telling each other about their summers. "I spent July in the village with my grandparents," says Taras. "I helped Grandpa in the garden and went fishing every morning. And you?" "We went to Odesa for two weeks," says Marichka. "I swam in the sea every day. Then I went to a dance camp near Kyiv. I learned three new dances!" Their friend Nazar joins them. He looks taller and has a new haircut. "I worked in my uncle's shop," he says proudly. "I earned some money and bought a new bike." The bell rings. Their class teacher, Ms Tkachuk, smiles at them. "Welcome back! This year we have some new subjects, a new computer room and two new students in our class." The new students are twins, Yeva and Danylo. They moved from Kharkiv in August. They look a little shy. "Hi! Do you want to sit with us?" asks Marichka. The twins smile. The new school year begins.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l1-after-the-bell-r: In our school, lessons finish at two o'clock, but many students stay longer. Our school has more than ten extracurricular activities, and each of them has its own fans. Ostap is the editor of the school newspaper. He writes articles, checks spelling and chooses photos. "It's my passion," he says. "I want to be a journalist one day." Solomiia spends every Tuesday in the science lab. The science club does real experiments there. "In class we learn the theory, but in the lab we see how it works," she explains. Bohdan plays the drums in the school band. The band practises twice a week and plays at every school concert. Yuliia collects old coins and stamps. She started a collectors' club last year, and now it has fifteen members. Some students combine two or three activities. Danylo, for example, plays in the band and writes for the newspaper. "It's not easy to fit in everything," he says, "but I never get bored." Our head teacher says that clubs help new students to fit in. You find friends who like the same things as you.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l2-my-clubs: Hi, I'm Mariia, and I'm twelve. My week is busy, but I like it that way. On Mondays I go to the drama club. We are preparing a play for the school festival in December. I play a fox, and I have a lot of funny lines. On Wednesdays I go to the robotics club. At first I was the only girl there, but now there are four of us. Last month our team built a robot that can sort rubbish. Our teacher wants to send it to a regional competition. On Fridays I have my favourite club, the volunteers' club. We help at the animal shelter near our school. I walk the dogs and clean the cages. My favourite dog is a big grey one called Smokey. Nobody wants to take him home because he is old, but he is the kindest dog in the world. My mum sometimes says I have too many clubs. But I always do my homework on time, so she doesn't really mind. Next year I want to try the school band. I can play the guitar a little.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l3-a-special-day-fo: This year our school is celebrating its fiftieth anniversary. Half a century! The whole school is preparing a big celebration, which we are going to dedicate to everybody who worked or studied here. Many graduates are coming back for the day. Some of them finished school forty years ago, and some only last summer. One of them is now a famous surgeon, and another is a pilot. They are going to make speeches about the importance of knowledge and good teachers. Every class is preparing something. The activities vary: the first-formers are singing, the fifth form is painting a long picture of the school's history, and our class is making a short film with old photos. In the old photos the uniforms look strange, and the classrooms look very different. But the students have one thing in common with us: they are smiling and laughing with their friends. "School spirit is not in the walls," our head teacher says. "It's in the people." I think she is right. The celebration is on Friday. I'm a little nervous, because I'm making a speech too.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l4-days-we-remember: Every school has its own special days. We asked students from three schools about their favourites. "In our school the most exciting day is Sports Day in May. The whole school goes to the stadium. There are races, games and a tug of war between teachers and students. The teachers usually lose!" Kyrylo, Lviv "My favourite is Knowledge Day on the first of September. The first-formers come with big bouquets, and an eleventh-former carries a little girl with a bell on her shoulder. Everybody cries a little, even the boys." Sofiia, Poltava "We have Book Day in March. Everybody comes dressed as a character from a book. Last year our maths teacher came as Harry Potter, and nobody could stop laughing. We also swap books, so everybody goes home with something new to read." Ilya, Vinnytsia "And the last bell in May is special too," adds Sofiia. "It's the last day for the eleventh-formers. It's happy and sad at the same time." What special days does your school have? Which one do you like most?
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l5-what-are-they-do: It is Wednesday, half past three. Lessons are over, but the school is still busy. Let's see what everybody is doing right now. In the gym the basketball team is training. They usually train on Mondays and Fridays, but today they are practising for a match on Saturday. In the music room Bohdan is playing the drums. He always practises after lessons because he can't play at home. His neighbours complain. In the library Ostap and Yuliia are working on the school newspaper. Ostap usually writes the articles, but today he is taking photos because the photographer is ill. In the canteen two first-formers are eating buns and waiting for their mums. They are drawing pictures on napkins. In the science lab Solomiia is doing an experiment with water and salt. She is writing the results in her notebook. And where is our head teacher? She is standing at the window of her office and watching the school yard. She does this every day at half past three. She says it is the best part of her day.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l6-a-day-in-two-liv: Meet two seventh-formers from two different places. Nastia lives in Kyiv. She gets up at seven and goes to school by underground. After school she goes to a swimming club three times a week. In the evenings she usually does her homework and chats with friends online. At weekends she often goes to the cinema. But this week is special. Nastia is staying with her cousin Mykola in a village near Zhytomyr. Today she is not going to the swimming pool. She is feeding chickens! Mykola gets up at six every day because he helps his parents on the farm before school. He walks to school with his friends. It takes twenty minutes. After school he plays football in the field behind the school. Right now Mykola is teaching Nastia to ride a horse. Nastia is holding the reins very carefully. She is laughing, but she is a bit scared. "In Kyiv I never see animals," she says. "Here everything is different." "And I never ride the underground," says Mykola. "Next summer I'm visiting you!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l7-join-our-club: Three students are talking in the school corridor about the club fair next week. Vlad: Guys, have you got anything in mind for the club fair? Ira: I think our eco-club should do something special. Last year we were stuck in a corner behind the stairs, and nobody saw us. Andrii: In my opinion, we need a big event. Something that everybody remembers. Vlad: Like what? Andrii: As for me, I'd like to make a giant robot out of plastic bottles. It can stand at the entrance and say, "Recycle me!" Ira: That's a great idea! We can also give away small plants in recycled cups. Vlad: And what about the chess club? We are always stuck with the boring table near the canteen. Ira: I think you should organise a mini tournament. The winner gets a chocolate medal. Vlad: Hmm, in my opinion chocolate is the best part. Okay, let's do it! On the day of the fair the robot was the star. More than thirty new students joined the eco-club, and twenty played in the chess tournament.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l8-sport-or-dance: Our school magazine asked: which is better for teenagers, sport or dance? Here are three answers. "I do judo three times a week. Sport teaches you to win and to lose. My coach says that your biggest opponent is yourself. When I win a fight, I feel strong and proud. When I lose, I learn something new." Maksym, 13 "I go to a folk dance group. We wear beautiful costumes and perform at festivals. Dance is like sport, believe me! After two hours of rehearsals my legs hurt. But on stage, when the music starts, I forget everything." Khrystyna, 12 "Why choose? I play volleyball and I also go to hip-hop classes. Volleyball is a team game, and hip-hop helps me to express myself. Both keep me fit, and both give me good friends." Roman, 13 Our PE teacher read the answers and smiled. "Sport or dance, it doesn't matter," she said. "The most important thing is to move and to enjoy it."
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l9-twenty-questions: Our English class played a game called "Twenty Questions". One student thinks of a hobby, and the others ask questions to guess it. Liza went first. She thought of a hobby. "What do you need for it?" asked Ivan. "You need paper and a pencil," said Liza. "Where do you usually do it?" asked Olena. "At home or outside, anywhere," answered Liza. "When did you start?" asked Pavlo. "When I was eight." "Why do you like it?" asked Mark. "Because it helps me to relax and to remember things." "How often do you do it?" asked Dasha. "Almost every day." "Who taught you?" asked Ivan. "My grandmother. She is an artist." "Is it drawing?" asked Olena. "Yes!" said Liza. Then it was Pavlo's turn. His hobby was harder: bird watching. It took fifteen questions! "Which birds do you see most often?" "What do you take with you?" "How long do you wait?" Finally somebody guessed. At the end the teacher said, "Look, you used every question word: what, where, when, why, how, who and which!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l10-what-does-our-c: Last week our class did a survey about free time. We asked all twenty-eight students in our form three questions: What do you do after school? How often do you do it? Who do you do it with? Here are the results. Nine students do sport. Football is the most popular, but three girls play basketball and one boy does karate. Seven students go to music school. Two of them play the piano, two play the violin, and three sing in a choir. Six students say their favourite free-time activity is gaming. They usually play online with friends for an hour or two in the evening. Our class teacher was not very happy about that result! Four students draw or paint. Iryna draws comics, and her comics are so good that we put them in the class newspaper. Only two students said they "do nothing". But when we asked again, one of them admitted that he walks his dog every day and helps his grandpa with the bees! We made a big chart with the results and put it on the classroom wall. Now everybody knows who to ask when they need a partner for football or a duet for the school concert.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l11-open-day-at-oak: Every school in Britain has its own traditions. At Oakfield School in Bristol, the most important day of the year is Open Day in June. On Open Day the school opens its doors to parents, grandparents and future students. Every department prepares something. In the science labs students show experiments with colourful liquids and small explosions (safe ones!). In the art room there is an exhibition of paintings and sculptures. The music department gives a concert in the hall. Students from Year 7, which is like our seventh form, work as guides. They wear special badges and show visitors around the school. "It's a big responsibility," says Amelia, 12. "You must know where everything is and answer lots of questions." In the afternoon there is a fair in the playground. Students sell cakes, old books and plants they have grown themselves. All the money goes to a charity. Last year they collected more than two thousand pounds for a children's hospital. At the end of the day the head teacher gives prizes to the best students of the year. "Open Day shows what our school is really like," she says. "It's not just lessons. It's people, ideas and friendship."
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l12-a-letter-from-a: Dear Oleksii, Thank you for your letter! It was great to read about your school in Chernihiv. Now let me tell you about mine. I go to a big school in Dublin, Ireland. There are more than a thousand students, so at first I got lost every day! Lessons start at nine and finish at half past three. My favourite subjects are history and PE. I don't like maths very much, but I'm getting better at it. After school I go to the hurling club. Hurling is a very old Irish sport. You play it with a wooden stick and a small ball. It's fast and a bit dangerous, but I love it. I also play the tin whistle in the school band. Right now I'm writing this letter in the library, because it's raining again. It rains a lot in Ireland! My friends are doing their homework next to me, and one of them is trying to read my letter. Tell me more about your clubs. What do you do at weekends? Do you have a school band? Which sports are popular in Ukraine? Write soon! Your friend, Cian
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l13-the-school-repo: Our school newspaper has a new section called "Meet the Teacher". This month our reporter, Vira from the seventh form, interviewed the new PE teacher, Mr Bondar. Vira: Where are you from, Mr Bondar? Mr Bondar: I'm from Ivano-Frankivsk, near the Carpathian Mountains. Vira: Why did you become a PE teacher? Mr Bondar: Because sport changed my life. When I was your age, I was very shy. Then I started skiing, and I found confidence and friends. Vira: What do you usually do at weekends? Mr Bondar: In winter I usually go skiing. In summer I go hiking with my family. Vira: What are you working on at the moment? Mr Bondar: I'm preparing a new club. It's a climbing club! We are building a climbing wall in the gym right now. Vira: How often will the club meet? Mr Bondar: Twice a week, on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Vira: Who can join? Mr Bondar: Everybody from the fifth form up. No experience needed, just good shoes and a brave heart! Vira says that after the interview she signed up first.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u1-l14-our-school-week: Hello! My name is Kateryna, and I'm the class monitor of 7-B. Our teacher asked me to describe a usual week in our class for our school website. On Mondays we start with English, and then we have a double maths lesson. Everybody is sleepy on Monday mornings, so our maths teacher always begins with a funny puzzle. On Tuesdays and Thursdays many of us stay after school for clubs. The robotics team, the choir and the football team all meet on these days. Wednesday is our "eco-day". Every Wednesday our class collects paper and plastic for recycling. Last year we collected four hundred kilograms of paper! Fridays are short. After lessons we often go to the park together or have a pizza at the café near the school. This week is different, though. We are preparing for the school anniversary concert. Right now the boys are learning a dance, and the girls are making decorations. Our class teacher is writing a short play, and I am helping her with the costumes. It's busy, but it's fun. I think our class is the best one in the school!
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l1-earning-pocket-m: How do teenagers earn pocket money? We asked four of them. "My parents pay me for extra chores. Washing up is part of my normal duties, so I don't get money for it. But if I hoover the whole flat or iron my dad's shirts, I get fifty hryvnias. I'm saving for new headphones." Liliia, 13 "I deliver leaflets for a pizza place on Saturday mornings. I walk about five kilometres! It's tiring, but I like being outside, and I earn my own money." Vadym, 14 "My parents are divorced, so I live with my mum during the week and with my dad at weekends. I split my chores between two homes. At Mum's I take out the garbage and feed the cat. At Dad's I help him in the garage." Olha, 12 "I don't get pocket money for chores. My parents say that everybody in a family must help for free. But I sell my old toys and books online, and I save everything." Denys, 13 So, should parents pay their children for chores? What do you think?
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l2-who-does-what: The Moroz family has five people and one big problem: housework. Last month Mum made a chart and put it on the fridge. Dad always cooks dinner on weekdays. He is a great cook, and he likes trying new recipes. He sometimes burns the potatoes, but nobody complains. Mum usually does the shopping and pays the bills. She never irons. "Life is too short for ironing," she says. Grandma lives with them. She always waters the plants and usually makes breakfast. She never washes up, because the family has a rule: whoever cooks doesn't wash up. Ivan, 13, takes out the garbage every evening and sometimes hoovers his room. He never makes his bed in the morning. "Why make it if I sleep in it again in the evening?" he asks. His sister Nina, 10, usually feeds the cat and always sets the table. She sometimes forgets to clean her teeth, but that's not housework! The chart works quite well. There are fewer arguments now, and everybody knows their duties.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l3-janes-kitchen-bl: Hi everyone, it's Jane again! Today I want to show you our kitchen, because yesterday something funny happened there. Our kitchen is small but cosy. There is a white tablecloth with red flowers on the table and an old teapot in the middle. It was my great-grandmother's teapot, and we only use it on special days. Next to the sink there is a dishwasher. Mum bought it last year, and since then we argue less about washing up! Yesterday Mum went to visit a friend, and I decided to cook pancakes for my little brothers. I took the big frying pan and a pot for the hot chocolate. I put the kettle on for Mum's tea, too. Everything went well until the first pancake. I tried to flip it in the air like a chef on TV. The pancake flew up and landed on the lamp! My brothers laughed so loudly that the neighbour knocked on the wall. In the end we had eleven good pancakes and one on the lamp. When Mum came home, she looked at the kitchen, then at the lamp, and said: "Next time, use a spatula!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l4-a-day-of-chores: Saturday is cleaning day in the Hrytsenko family. Everybody has a job, and nobody can go out until the flat is clean. At nine o'clock Dad opens all the windows. "Fresh air first!" he says. Then he hoovers the carpets in the living room and the hall. Mum cleans the bathroom and the kitchen. She is fast and very careful. She says that a clean kitchen is a healthy kitchen. Bohdana, 12, dusts the shelves and waters the plants. She has a lot of plants in her room, about twenty, so this job takes half an hour. Her brother Lev, 14, changes the sheets on all the beds and takes the old newspapers and bottles to the recycling bins. At twelve o'clock the family meets in the kitchen. They check the list on the fridge. Every job has a tick. Then Dad makes his famous Saturday omelette, and everybody eats together. "I hate cleaning," says Lev, "but I love the feeling when it's finished. The flat looks new, and the rest of the weekend is free!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l5-when-mum-was-awa: Last week Mum went on a business trip for three days, and Dad stayed at home with Yurii, 13, and his sister Zlata, 8. When Mum came back, she had a lot of questions. "Did you eat properly?" Mum asked. "Yes, we did," said Dad. "We ate pasta on Monday, pasta on Tuesday and... pasta on Wednesday." "Did anybody wash up?" "Yes, Yurii did. Every evening!" Mum looked surprised. Yurii smiled proudly. "What did you do on Tuesday evening?" "We watched a film and made popcorn," said Zlata. "Dad burned the first bowl." "Where did the cat sleep?" "In my bed," said Zlata. "She was lonely without you." "Why is there a sock on the kitchen lamp?" Silence. Then everybody laughed. "We played sock basketball," Yurii explained. "Dad won." "And did you do your homework?" "Of course we did!" said Yurii quickly. Mum looked around. The flat was not perfect, but it was clean, the plants were alive, and everybody was happy. "Well done," she said. "Next time I'll leave you a cookbook."
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l6-two-families-two: Sofiia from Lutsk and Harry from Manchester are pen friends. Last month they compared housework in their families. In Sofiia's family everybody has fixed duties. Her mum cooks, her dad does the repairs, and Sofiia and her brother clean their rooms and wash up in turns. On Sundays the whole family cleans the flat together, and then they have a big family lunch. "My grandma visits every week and checks my room," Sofiia writes. "If it's messy, I hear about it for an hour!" Harry's family works differently. Every Sunday evening they write a list of jobs for the week on a whiteboard in the kitchen. Then everybody chooses jobs. Harry usually chooses cooking, because he loves making curry. His younger sister prefers looking after the garden and the rabbit. "We don't have fixed duties," Harry writes, "but if somebody forgets a job, they must do an extra one next week." Both friends agree on one thing: when everybody helps, the house is nicer and parents are less tired. And both of them hate cleaning the bathroom!
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l7-home-helpers: Last month our class visited a small museum of household appliances in our town. It was much more interesting than we expected. In the first room there were very old things. We saw a heavy iron which people heated on the stove, and a wooden washing board. "Imagine washing all your family's clothes by hand," said the guide. "It took a whole day!" In the second room there were the first electrical appliances. The first vacuum cleaner looked like a big metal box on wheels. The first washing machine had no programmes, only one button. There was also an old toaster that could toast only one slice of bread at a time. The third room showed modern appliances. There was a microwave oven that can talk, a robot vacuum cleaner and a hairdryer that is as quiet as a whisper. At the end the guide showed us her favourite thing, an old electric saw. "Every new appliance was an improvement," she said. "Each one gave people more free time." On the way home Maksym said, "I think the dishwasher is the best invention. I hate washing up!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l8-when-the-lights-: Last Friday there was a big storm in our town. At exactly seven o'clock in the evening all the lights went out. What was everybody in our family doing at that moment? Mum was ironing a shirt in the bedroom. Dad was cooking dinner in the kitchen. He was frying potatoes, and the kitchen smelled wonderful. My sister Yaryna was drying her hair with a hairdryer. She was singing, too, very loudly. Grandpa was sitting in his armchair. He was reading a newspaper and listening to the radio. And me? I was hoovering my room. Well, I wasn't really hoovering. I was playing a game on my phone, and the vacuum cleaner was just making noise. Suddenly everything went dark and quiet. For a second nobody said anything. Then Grandpa laughed. "Now everybody can see what everybody was really doing!" We lit candles, sat in the kitchen and finished Dad's potatoes. The lights came back after two hours, but nobody wanted to turn on the TV. It was one of the best evenings of the year.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l9-notes-on-the-fri: In the Shevchuk family everybody is busy, so they talk through notes on the fridge. Here are the notes from last Monday. Andrii, please take out the garbage before school. And don't forget your PE kit! Love, Mum. Mum, I'm at football practice until six. I took my PE kit, don't worry. There's no bread, by the way. Andrii. Kids, I'm working late today. There is soup in the fridge. Warm it up in the microwave, don't use the oven. Dad. Dad, the soup was delicious! I washed the pot and fed the cat. Can I go to Olia's house on Saturday? Her mum says it's OK. Ira. Ira, yes, you can go, but first tidy your room. It looks like a storm was there! Mum. Everybody, Grandma is coming on Wednesday! Let's clean the flat on Tuesday evening, OK? And somebody buy bread!!! Dad. I bought bread. Two loaves. Andrii. Mum keeps the funniest notes in a box. She says that one day they will be the family's history.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l10-a-job-for-today: Every Saturday Petro, 13, has an unusual job. He helps his neighbour, Mrs Halyna, who is eighty-two and lives alone on the fifth floor. "It started last winter," Petro says. "I saw her on the stairs with heavy bags. The lift wasn't working. I took the bags and carried them up. Since then I help her every week." Petro does her shopping, takes out her garbage and sometimes changes a light bulb. Mrs Halyna can't stand on a chair any more. Last month he helped her to hang new curtains. Mrs Halyna doesn't let him leave without tea and cherry pie. She tells him stories about her life. She was a geography teacher for forty years and visited many countries. "I think everybody should help elderly people," Petro says. "It doesn't take much time, and they are really interesting to talk to. Mrs Halyna knows more about the world than the internet!" Petro's parents are proud of him. Now two of his friends help other neighbours in their building too.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l11-a-robot-for-eve: Our English teacher asked us to write about chores in the future. Here is my essay. In the future, every home will have a robot helper. I'm sure of it. My robot will be called Bob, and he will do all the chores I hate. In the morning Bob will make my bed and cook breakfast. He will use the toaster, the kettle and the frying pan at the same time, because he will have six arms. While I am at school, Bob will hoover the flat, wash the clothes and iron them. He will also water Mum's plants and walk our dog, Bublyk. Bublyk will probably bark at him at first, but they will become friends. In the evening Bob will help me with my homework. Well, maybe not. Mum says I must do it myself. But I have one worry. If robots do all the chores, what will people do? Will we become lazy? My grandma says that housework teaches you to be responsible. So maybe I will keep one chore for myself. I will wash up, because I like playing with the bubbles. Everything else is Bob's job!
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l12-chores-around-t: Do children in other countries do the same chores as you? Here are some interesting facts. In Japan, students clean their own schools. Every day after lunch they sweep the floors, clean the windows and even wash the toilets. There are almost no cleaners in Japanese schools. Japanese people believe that this teaches respect and teamwork. In Kenya, many children in villages help to fetch water. Sometimes the river or the well is far from home, so they carry heavy containers for kilometres. In Sweden, parents and children often share chores equally. Boys and girls do the same jobs, and fathers cook as often as mothers. In Mexico, children often help their grandparents. Big families live together, and teenagers look after younger cousins. In Ukraine, many children help their grandparents in the garden in summer. They pick strawberries, water the vegetables and feed the chickens. Chores are different, but the idea is the same everywhere: a home is a team, and every member helps.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l13-a-messy-weekend: Hi Lukas, Thanks for your email! You asked about housework in my family. Well, last weekend was a real disaster, so let me tell you about it. On Saturday my parents went to a wedding in Uzhhorod, and my older brother Vitalii and I stayed at home alone for the first time. Mum left us a long list of chores. On Saturday morning we were watching cartoons when Vitalii suddenly remembered the list. We quickly started. I was washing up, and Vitalii was putting clothes into the washing machine. Unfortunately, he put my white T-shirt together with his new red socks. Now I have a pink T-shirt! In the afternoon, while I was hoovering, Vitalii was cooking pasta. The water boiled over and covered the whole cooker. On Sunday we worked for six hours to clean everything. When our parents came home, the flat was clean and the pink T-shirt was hiding in my wardrobe. Mum read the list, looked around and said, "Well done! Next time you can stay alone for a week." I'm not sure that's a good idea! What chores do you do at home? Write soon! Best wishes, Taras
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u2-l14-who-broke-the-w: On Sunday morning the Kravets family found the washing machine full of water and silent. It was broken. Who did it? Mum decided to find out. "What were you doing yesterday evening?" she asked everybody. "I was doing my homework," said Oleh, 13. "Then I watched a football match." "I was reading in my room," said his sister Mila, 11. "I didn't go near the bathroom." "I was fixing the bike in the garage," said Dad. "I was there all evening." Mum looked at everybody carefully. Then she noticed something. Mila's hair was wet, and there was a small blue shoe on the bathroom floor. "Mila, did you wash something yesterday?" Mila went red. "Only my doll's clothes," she said quietly. "And... maybe my trainers." "Your trainers? In the washing machine?" Mum couldn't believe it. "Didn't you see the instructions?" "No," said Mila. "I was in a hurry. I was going to a birthday party and my trainers were dirty." In the end Dad fixed the machine. He found a shoelace in it. Since then Mila reads all the instructions very carefully.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l1-table-manners-ar: Imagine you are having dinner in another country. Do you know how to behave? Table manners are very different around the world, and what is polite in one place can be rude in another. In China and Japan people eat with chopsticks. Never stick your chopsticks straight up in a bowl of rice: people consider it very bad luck. In Bangladesh and in parts of India many people eat with their hands, but only with the right hand. The left hand is not used for food. In Britain people expect you to keep your hands on the table, not on your lap, and to say "please" and "thank you" all the time. In Korea the oldest person at the table starts eating first. Young people wait to show respect. And what about technology? In many families today, phones and other devices are not allowed at the table. "Dinner is for talking," says a mum from Kharkiv. "No item of technology can be more important than family." In Ukraine the host always serves too much food, and guests should try everything. If you leave an empty plate, you'll probably get more!
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l2-lunch-for-four: It's Saturday. Mum and Dad are at work, and Marta, 13, has promised to cook lunch for herself, her brother Bohdan and two friends who are coming at one o'clock. Marta: Bohdan, what do we have in the fridge? Bohdan: Let me see. Eggs, cheese, tomatoes, some chicken and a cucumber. And there's rice in the cupboard. Marta: Great! We can make chicken with rice and a salad. Bohdan: Can I help? I can wash the vegetables. Marta: Yes, please. Wash the tomatoes and the cucumber, and then cut them. Be careful with the knife! Bohdan: What are you doing with the chicken? Marta: I'm cutting it into small pieces. Then I'll fry it with onion. Can you put the rice in the pot? Two cups of rice and four cups of water. Bohdan: Done! What about dessert? Marta: There are apples. Let's bake them with honey and cinnamon. At one o'clock the doorbell rang. The friends came in and smelled the kitchen. "Wow! Did your mum cook this?" asked Dmytro. "No," said Bohdan proudly. "We did!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l3-the-food-artist: Some people paint on canvas. Some people carve wood or stone. But Ilona Shpak from Odesa uses a very unusual material: food. Ilona carves watermelons, pumpkins and even cheese. With a small knife she can turn a watermelon into a rose, a swan or a portrait of a person. One watermelon takes her about three hours. It all started when she was fifteen. She saw a photo of a carved melon on the internet and wondered, "Can I do that?" Her first try was a disaster, and her family ate the mistake for dessert. But she didn't stop. Today Ilona is a professional food artist. Restaurants and hotels hire her for weddings and big parties. Food companies ask her to promote their products, and she has thousands of followers online. "People often ask me if it's sad when they eat my work," she says. "No! Food is for eating. My art lives for one evening, and then it makes people happy and full." Her advice for beginners is simple: "Start with an apple and a teaspoon. And don't be afraid of mistakes. You can always eat them!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l4-have-you-ever-tr: Our school has an exchange programme, and this year three students from other countries are studying with us. In our English lesson we asked them about Ukrainian food. Lucia from Spain: "I have tried borshch, and I love it! I have eaten varenyky with cherries too. But I have never tried salo. It looks a bit scary." Kenji from Japan: "I have tasted many Ukrainian dishes, and my favourite is holubtsi. I have also learned to make syrnyky with my host family. In Japan we don't eat so much sour cream!" Emma from Canada: "I have just eaten my first kutia. It was sweet and very unusual. I haven't tried uzvar yet, but my friends say it's delicious." Then they asked us questions. "Have you ever eaten sushi?" asked Kenji. Most of the class said yes. "Have you ever tried paella?" asked Lucia. Only three students said yes. "And have you ever had poutine?" asked Emma. Nobody knew what it was! It's chips with cheese and gravy, a famous Canadian dish. At the end we decided to have an international food day next month.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l5-grandpas-grilled: My grandpa is a fisherman, and his favourite recipe is grilled salmon. Last Sunday he taught me how to make it. Here is the recipe. You need: two salmon fillets, one lemon, a few sprigs of fresh dill and oregano, two spoons of olive oil, one spoon of apple vinegar, salt and pepper. First, make the mixture. Squeeze the lemon into a bowl. Pour in the olive oil and the vinegar. Cut the dill and oregano into small pieces and add them. Add salt and pepper and mix everything well. Next, put the salmon fillets on a plate and pour the mixture over them. Leave them for twenty minutes. Then grill the salmon for about five minutes on each side. If you don't have a grill, you can fry it in a frying pan. Finally, let the fish cool down a little. Serve it with potatoes and a fresh salad. "The secret," says Grandpa, "is fresh fish and a happy cook." Our salmon was delicious. Even my little sister, who hates fish, asked for more!
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l6-the-class-cook-o: Last Friday our class had a cooking competition in the school canteen. We worked in four teams, and each team had one hour to cook a dish. Team 1 made pizza. They made the dough themselves, which was a bit risky, but it worked. The pizza had cheese, mushrooms and lots of tomato sauce. Team 2 cooked deruny, Ukrainian potato pancakes. Danylo grated the potatoes so fast that the judges were amazed. They served the deruny with sour cream. Team 3 decided to make a fruit salad. It looked like a rainbow: strawberries, oranges, bananas, kiwis and blueberries. Simple, but beautiful. Team 4, my team, made chocolate muffins. We nearly had a disaster when Olia forgot the sugar. Luckily, Roman noticed it just in time. The judges were our head teacher, the canteen cook and the school nurse. They tasted everything carefully. In the end Team 2 won with their deruny. Team 4 got a special prize for "Best Teamwork". The canteen cook liked the competition so much that she now wants to put the winning deruny on the school menu!
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l7-an-interview-wit: Ivanna Moroz is only fifteen, but she has already won two cooking competitions and has her own cooking channel. Our school reporter asked her some questions. How long have you cooked? Since I was seven. My grandma taught me to make varenyky, and I've loved cooking ever since. What is the most difficult dish you have made? A French cake with six layers. It took me two days, and I've made it only once! How many videos have you made? About a hundred and twenty. My little brother films them on his phone. Which countries' food have you tried to cook? Italian, Georgian, Mexican and Thai. Thai food is my favourite now. Where have you travelled with your cooking? I've cooked at food festivals in Lviv and Kyiv. Last year I went to a competition in Poland. Why have you chosen cooking? Because food brings people together. When I cook for my family, everybody sits at one table and talks. What have you learned from your mistakes? That burned pancakes are not the end of the world!
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l8-safe-in-the-kitc: The kitchen is the most dangerous room in the house. It has knives, hot water, fire and electricity. Here is a conversation between Mr Lysenko, a cooking teacher, and his new students. Mr Lysenko: Before we start, what are the rules in the kitchen? Dariia: Wash your hands before you touch food. Mr Lysenko: Good. What else? Kostia: Don't run with a knife! Mr Lysenko: Exactly. Always carry a knife with the point down. And what about hot pots? Olesia: Use oven gloves. And turn the handles of pots to the back of the cooker, so nobody can knock them over. Mr Lysenko: Very good. What should you do if oil in a frying pan catches fire? Kostia: Pour water on it? Mr Lysenko: No! Never put water on burning oil. It makes the fire bigger. Cover the pan with a lid and turn off the cooker. Dariia: And keep paper and towels away from the cooker. Mr Lysenko: Perfect. One more rule: always clean up after yourself. A clean kitchen is a safe kitchen. At the end of the lesson nobody was hurt, and the vegetable soup was excellent.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l9-a-picnic-in-the-: The weather forecast said sunny and warm, so Sasha and her friends decided to have a picnic in the park on Sunday. Each friend agreed to bring something. Sasha made sandwiches with cheese, ham and cucumber. She cut them into triangles because they look nicer that way. Maksym brought a big bottle of lemonade. He made it himself with lemons, mint and honey. It was a bit too sour, but nobody complained. Polina baked a cherry pie the evening before. It was still a little warm when she brought it. Artem's job was the fruit. He brought apples, grapes and a watermelon, but he forgot a knife! They had to borrow one from a family at the next table. Diana brought the blanket, paper plates and a bag for rubbish. "We must leave the park clean," she said. They ate, played badminton, laughed and took lots of photos. At five o'clock they collected all the rubbish and went home. "Next time," said Artem, "I'm bringing bananas. You don't need a knife for bananas!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l10-a-taste-of-ukra: Every region of Ukraine has its own special dishes. If you travel around the country, your stomach will be very happy! Borshch is the most famous Ukrainian dish. There are dozens of recipes, and every family thinks theirs is the best. In Poltava they add small dumplings called halushky. In the west some families make a clear red borshch for Christmas Eve. Varenyky are popular everywhere. People fill them with potatoes, cabbage, cheese or cherries. In summer cherry varenyky with sour cream are a real treat. In the Carpathians you must try banosh. People make it from cornmeal and sour cream and cook it over a fire. People serve it with mushrooms and brynza, a salty sheep's cheese. In Crimea the Crimean Tatars cook chebureky and yantyky, crispy pies with meat. Many Ukrainians love them. And for dessert? Try Kyiv cake, with nuts, meringue and cream. People bring it as a present when they visit friends. Ukrainian food is simple, filling and made with love. As our grandmothers say: "Eat, eat, you are too thin!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l11-the-best-caf-in: Our class newspaper has a food column. This month Maryna, 13, visited a new café called "Honey Bear" and wrote a review. "Honey Bear opened in our town last month, and there is always a queue. I went there with my parents on Saturday to find out why. The café is small and cosy, with wooden tables and plants everywhere. On the walls there are photos of bees and old honey jars. It smells of fresh bread and cinnamon. The menu is not very long, but everything sounds delicious. I ordered pancakes with honey and berries, and a hot chocolate. My dad chose a mushroom omelette, and my mum had a vegetable soup with fresh bread. The pancakes were soft and warm, and the berries were fresh. The hot chocolate was a bit too sweet for me, but my dad loved it. The soup was the best part of the meal, my mum says. The waiters were friendly and fast, even though the café was full. Prices are fair: a meal for three cost about the same as a pizza. My score: 9 out of 10. Next time I want to try the honey cake!"
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u3-l12-my-food-diary: Our biology teacher asked us to keep a food diary for one week. It's Thursday evening, and this is what I have written so far. This week I have eaten a lot of fruit. I have had an apple every day, and yesterday I tried a mango for the first time. It was sweet and juicy! I have drunk more water than usual. Our teacher says we need about six glasses a day. I haven't reached six yet, but I've drunk four or five every day. I have already eaten fish twice: salmon on Monday and fish soup today. I have never liked fish much, but Mum's fish soup is changing my mind. Unfortunately, I have also eaten too many sweets. My friend has just had a birthday, and there was a huge chocolate cake. I've had three pieces this week! I haven't eaten any fast food yet, and I'm proud of that. Usually I have burgers twice a week. What have I learned? Healthy food can be tasty. And keeping a diary makes you think before you eat that fourth piece of cake.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u4-l1-the-star-over-be: Christmas is one of the most important holidays in many countries. It celebrates the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem more than two thousand years ago. But every nation has its own way to celebrate it. In Ukraine Christmas Eve is a family evening. People wait for the first star in the sky, and then the family sits down to a supper of twelve dishes. The most important dish is kutia, made of wheat, honey, poppy seeds and nuts. The day after, children go carolling. They sing old songs called koliadky and receive sweets and money. Many Ukrainian traditions have a link to the land and to the year of a farmer. The didukh, a sheaf of wheat in the corner of the room, represents the spirits of the family and a good harvest. Some families go to a midnight mass. Others decorate their homes with embroidered towels with old patterns. Every region has its own pattern, and some families believe that each pattern belongs to their own family. What do all these traditions have in common? Goodness, family and hope. They define who we are. Even people who are not religious relate to these traditions, because they connect us with our grandparents.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u4-l2-a-year-of-holida: Our class made a calendar of holidays for the classroom wall. Each student chose one month and wrote about a holiday. Here are some of them. January: Christmas and New Year are over, but on the 22nd of January we celebrate the Day of Unity of Ukraine. February: On the 14th of February people give cards and flowers to people they love. It's Valentine's Day. March: On the 8th of March many people give flowers to their mothers, grandmothers and teachers. April or May: Easter is a moving holiday, so the date changes every year. We paint pysanky and take Easter baskets to church. June: On the 1st of June we celebrate Children's Day. Many towns have concerts and games in the parks. August: On the 24th of August we celebrate Independence Day. People wear embroidered shirts, called vyshyvankas, and people decorate the cities with blue and yellow flags. December: On the 6th of December we have St Nicholas Day. Children find small presents under their pillows in the morning, but only if they were good! "What is your favourite holiday?" our teacher asked. Most students said St Nicholas Day. Presents under the pillow are hard to beat!
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u4-l3-happy-new-year-a: At midnight on the 31st of December, people all over the world welcome the New Year. But the traditions are very different. In Spain people eat twelve grapes at midnight, one grape for each stroke of the clock. Each grape represents a lucky month. It's harder than it sounds! In Denmark people smash old plates on the doors of their friends' houses. According to tradition, the more broken plates you find in the morning, the more friends you have. In Colombia some people walk around the block with an empty suitcase. They hope that the new year will bring lots of travel. In Scotland the first person who enters your house after midnight is very important. A tall, dark-haired man with a piece of coal brings good luck. In Japan bells in Buddhist temples ring 108 times to clean away the bad things of the old year. In Ukraine families decorate a New Year tree, cook a big dinner and watch fireworks. At midnight everybody makes a wish.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u4-l4-how-pysanky-are-: Pysanky are decorated Easter eggs, and they are one of the most famous symbols of Ukraine. They are made with wax and natural dyes, and every pattern has a meaning. First, a raw egg is washed and dried. Then a pattern is drawn on the egg with hot wax. A special tool called a kistka is used for this. Next, the egg is put into a light dye, usually yellow. The parts with wax stay white. Then more wax is added, and the egg is put into a darker dye, for example red. This is repeated several times. At the end the wax is melted near a candle and removed. Suddenly all the colours appear. It's like magic! In the past, pysanky were made only by women, often at night when the children were asleep. Each pattern was kept in the family and passed from mother to daughter. The symbols are very old. A sun means life, a wave means water, and wheat means a good harvest. Today pysanky are collected all over the world. There is even a giant pysanka in Kolomyia. It is a museum, and it is visited by thousands of people every year.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u4-l5-christmas-in-bri: Christmas in Britain is celebrated on the 25th of December. Preparations start weeks before. Houses are decorated with lights, and evergreen plants, like holly and ivy, are hung over doors and fireplaces. The Christmas tree is covered with shiny balls and lights. On Christmas Eve children hang stockings by the fireplace. They believe that Father Christmas comes down the chimney at night and fills the stockings with presents. Children usually leave a mince pie and a carrot for him and his reindeer. On Christmas Day the family has a big dinner with roast turkey, potatoes and vegetables. Before the meal everybody pulls a cracker. It's a paper tube which makes a loud bang. Inside there is a paper crown, a small toy and a joke. In Scotland, New Year is even more important than Christmas. It's called Hogmanay. At the last stroke of midnight people hold hands and sing "Auld Lang Syne", an old song about friendship written by the poet Robert Burns. Many families also provide food and presents for people who are alone or poor at Christmas. For many British people, that is the real spirit of Christmas.
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u4-l6-christmas-quiz-n: On the last Friday before the winter holidays our English club had a Christmas quiz night. The quizmaster was our teacher, Ms Koval, in a red hat. "Christmas in Ukraine is on the 25th of December, isn't it?" she asked first. "Yes, it is!" everybody shouted. "Father Christmas doesn't come down the chimney in Ukraine, does he?" "No, he doesn't! St Nicholas puts presents under our pillows!" "You've all made pysanky, haven't you?" Some students said yes, some said no. "That's an Easter tradition anyway!" laughed Vova. Then teams answered harder questions about Christmas in other countries. Team Snowflakes knew that people in Australia often celebrate Christmas on the beach, because it's summer there. Team Reindeer knew that in Norway people hide their brooms on Christmas Eve, so witches can't steal them. The last question was a crossword. The teams had to find ten Christmas words: star, carol, candle, gift, angel, snow, tree, bell, wish and kutia. In the end Team Reindeer won by one point. Their prize was a big box of gingerbread biscuits, which they shared with everybody. That was a nice ending, wasn't it?
k6aud/_final_k7t1|u4-l7-the-first-thanks: Not all holidays are about winter. In the USA one of the most important holidays is Thanksgiving, on the fourth Thursday of November. Its history goes back four centuries. In 1620 a group of English settlers sailed to America on a ship called the Mayflower. The journey was dreadful: it lasted more than two months, and many people were ill. Their first winter was very hard, and half of them died. The local Native Americans showed the settlers how to grow corn and where to catch fish. In autumn 1621, after a good harvest, the settlers and the Native Americans had a big meal together. It lasted three days. This is remembered as the first Thanksgiving. Today families get together and eat roast turkey with gravy, cranberry sauce and pumpkin pie. Before the meal many families say a blessing or tell each other what they are thankful for. In Ukraine we have a different tradition of giving thanks for food: Lent. Before Easter many people give up meat, milk or sweets for some weeks. When Easter comes, the first meal tastes like the best meal of the year. Both traditions teach the same thing: be thankful for what you have.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l1-sports-news: Welcome to "Sports Minute", our school radio's weekly news! Here are this week's top stories. Baseball: Ukrainian player Andrii Koval has signed a contract with a team in the USA. He usually plays as a shortstop, but sometimes as a second baseman. "I want to keep up with the best players in the world," he told reporters. Football: In an exciting match last night, the Ukrainian youth team defeated Uruguay 2:1. Uruguay scored first, but our team turned out to be stronger in the second half. The winning goal came in the last minute! Swimming: At the European Junior Championship, fifteen-year-old Daryna Melnyk won a bronze medal in the 200 metres. She trains in a small pool in her hometown and gets up at five every morning. School sport: And finally, news from our own gym. Our basketball team played against School No. 12 on Friday. The match turned out to be very close. We lost by just two points, but our captain, Taras from 7-A, scored twenty points! That's all for this week. Keep moving, and see you next Monday!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l2-is-sport-only-fo: After the sports news on our school radio, our class had a hot discussion: should school sport be about winning, or about having fun? "Winning is important," said Bohdan, who plays in the school football team. "If you don't want to win, why do you play? Competition makes you stronger." "I don't agree," said Nastia. "I'm not very good at sport, and in PE lessons nobody wants me in their team. That's why many students hate PE. Sport should be for everybody." "I think both are important," said Yurii. "In a match you should try to win. But at school the main thing is to move and enjoy it." Our PE teacher listened and then gave an example. "Last year the slowest runner in the school ran in the charity race. She finished last, but everybody cheered for her. She was the real hero of the day." Then she made a decision. Next month our school will have a new "Fun Sports Day": no medals, no points, just funny team games like sack races and three-legged races. "And the teachers will run too!" she added. Everybody laughed.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l3-unusual-sports: Football, tennis and athletics are popular everywhere. But have you heard of these unusual sports? Zorbing: You get inside a giant transparent ball and roll down a hill. It was invented in New Zealand. It's not dangerous, but you can feel a bit sick! Underwater hockey: Players wear masks and fins and push a small puck along the bottom of a swimming pool with short sticks. You must hold your breath and play at the same time. Cycle ball: It's like football, but on bicycles. Players hit the ball with the front wheel. It's very popular in Germany and Switzerland. Elephant polo: Players sit on elephants and hit a ball with very long sticks. It's played in Nepal and Thailand. The elephants are gentle and well looked after. Windsurfing is not so unusual, but it's very hard. You stand on a board and hold a sail. The wind pulls you across the water. And what about the more traditional ones? Wrestling and weightlifting are some of the oldest sports in the world. People did them at the first Olympic Games in ancient Greece. Which sport would you like to try?
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l4-the-olympic-drea: The Olympic Games are the biggest sports event in the world. The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896. Only about 240 athletes, all men, competed in nine disciplines. Today more than ten thousand athletes from over two hundred countries compete in the Summer Games. There are more than thirty sports, from athletics and swimming to rowing and skateboarding. The Winter Games are held two years after the Summer Games. The Olympic motto is "Faster, Higher, Stronger, Together". The five rings on the flag represent five continents, joined in friendship. After the Olympic Games come the Paralympic Games, for athletes with a disability. They are held in the same city, and the athletes are just as brave and strong. Swimmers, wheelchair basketball players and blind football players amaze the world. Ukraine first appeared at the Olympic Games as an independent country in 1994. Since then Ukrainian athletes have won many medals. Our Paralympic team is one of the strongest in the world and often finishes in the top five. Every young athlete dreams about representing their country at the Olympics one day.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l5-when-was-it-inve: Many sports that we play today are quite young. Here is a short history of some of them. Basketball was invented in 1891 by James Naismith, a teacher in the USA. His students needed a game for the cold winter. The first baskets were made from peach baskets, so after every goal somebody had to climb a ladder and take the ball out! Volleyball was created four years later, in 1895, by another teacher, William Morgan. He wanted a game that was gentler than basketball for older people. The rules of modern football were written in England in 1863. Before that, every school played with its own rules, and some matches were very rough. Table tennis was first played in Britain in the 1880s. People played it after dinner on dining tables, with books as a net and a champagne cork as a ball. Snowboarding was invented in the 1960s in the USA. At first it was called "snurfing". It was added to the Olympic Games in 1998. Who knows? Maybe the next popular sport will be invented by somebody in your class!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l6-water-sports: Summer is the best time for water sports. We asked three teenagers about their favourites. "I go kayaking on the Dnipro with my dad. We paddle for two or three hours and stop on little islands for a picnic. You must always wear a life jacket, even if you can swim well." Mykhailo, 13 "My sport is synchronised swimming. It looks easy and beautiful, but it's really hard. We hold our breath, move together and smile at the same time! We train six days a week." Olesia, 12 "Last summer I learned to surf in Portugal. I fell off the board about a hundred times on the first day. On the third day I finally stood up and rode a small wave. It was the best moment of my life!" Denys, 14 Our swimming coach gave some safety tips: never swim alone, don't swim after a big meal, and always listen to the lifeguard. "Water is a friend," she says, "but you must respect it."
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l7-where-do-you-pla: Every sport has its own place and its own equipment. Do you know them all? Football is played on a pitch. The players try to kick the ball into the goal. A goalkeeper stands in the goal and tries to stop them. Ice hockey is played on a rink. Instead of a ball, players hit a small black puck with a stick. Players skate very fast, and the game can be quite rough. Tennis and basketball are both played on a court. In tennis there is a net in the middle. In basketball there is a basket at each end, and players throw the ball through it. Volleyball also has a net, but it's much higher than in tennis. You can play volleyball inside on a court or outside on the beach. In Ukraine, football is the most popular team sport. But our hockey and basketball teams have many fans too. Next time you watch a match, look at the place and the equipment. You will understand the game much better!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l8-a-stadium-with-a: Our town has an old stadium near the river. Last week our class went on a tour there, and we learned a lot of interesting facts. The stadium was built in 1936. At first it was just a field with wooden benches. The stands were made of wood, and only two thousand people could sit there. In 1965 the old wooden stands were replaced with concrete ones. Lights were added, so matches could be played in the evening. In 1980 the first running track was opened. Many famous Ukrainian athletes were trained there when they were young. The stadium was damaged by a big flood in 1998, but it was repaired by the people of the town. Volunteers worked every weekend for four months! In 2015 the stadium was modernised. New seats were installed, and a new gym was built under the stands. Today the stadium is used by school teams, a football club and a running club. Every year on Independence Day a big concert is held there. "This stadium is the heart of our town," our guide said. We agreed.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l9-whats-your-sport: Two new classmates, Kateryna and Ali, are talking during the break. Kateryna: So, Ali, do you do any sport? Ali: Yes, I play cricket. It's very popular in Pakistan, where my family is from. Kateryna: Cricket? I've never seen it. Is it like baseball? Ali: A bit. There's a bat and a ball, and two teams. But a match can last five days! Kateryna: Five days? That's crazy! I prefer something faster. I do fencing. Ali: Fencing? With swords? Kateryna: Yes, but they aren't sharp. We wear white suits and masks. It's like a chess game, but with your body. You must think very fast. Ali: That sounds cool! How long have you done it? Kateryna: Four years. I train three times a week. Ali: Could I come and watch one day? Kateryna: Sure! Come on Thursday. And maybe you can teach me cricket one day. But not for five days! They both laughed. The bell rang, and they ran to their maths lesson.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l10-join-a-sports-c: Our town's youth sports centre has started its new season. Here are some of the clubs for teenagers. Rock climbing: Tuesdays and Thursdays, 5-7 pm. For ages 11-16. Climb our new 12-metre wall! All equipment is provided. Bring sports clothes and good energy. Table tennis: Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, 4-6 pm. All ages. Our coach is a former national champion. Tournament every last Saturday of the month. Girls' football: Saturdays, 10-12 am. For ages 12-15. Our team won the city cup last year! New players are always welcome. Archery: Sundays, 11 am-1 pm. For ages 13+. Learn to shoot with a real bow. Safety first: parents must sign a form. Dance fitness: Mondays and Thursdays, 6-7 pm. Fun, music and movement for everyone. No experience needed. Membership costs 300 hryvnias a month for one club. Each extra club is 150 hryvnias. Your first lesson is free, so come and try! Call us or visit us at 15 Sadova Street.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l11-football-heroes: Football is the most popular sport in Ukraine, and our country has given the world some great players. One of the most famous is Andriy Shevchenko. He started playing for Dynamo Kyiv as a teenager, and later he played in Italy and England. In 2004 he won the Ballon d'Or, the prize for the best footballer in Europe. Another legend is Oleh Blokhin. He won the Ballon d'Or in 1975 and was famous for his amazing speed. But football heroes are not only men. The Ukrainian women's national team is growing stronger every year, and many young girls now play in football schools. Today many young Ukrainian players play in top clubs in Spain, England and Germany. When they score, the whole country celebrates. Football is also about fans. When the national team plays, people meet in cafés and squares, wear yellow and blue shirts and sing together. Coaches say that the most important thing for young players is not talent but hard work. "Talent opens the door," one coach said, "but only work keeps you inside."
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l12-the-sports-day-: Last Friday our school had its spring Sports Day. Here are the results from our class, 7-B. In the 100-metre race Maksym finished first, Ivan was second and Oleh was third. Maksym ran it in 13.4 seconds, a new class record! In the long jump Sofiia jumped 4 metres 10 centimetres and won a gold medal. "I've trained for this all winter," she said happily. In the relay race our team was unlucky. Roman dropped the baton, and we finished fourth. But we cheered for him, and he smiled again. In the tug of war we beat 7-A in thirty seconds. It was the fastest win of the day. The funniest event was the teachers' race. Our maths teacher was the fastest, but our English teacher stopped to help a first-former who fell down. Everybody clapped for her. In total, our class won three gold medals, two silver and one bronze. We finished second in the school table, just one point behind 7-A. Next year we'll beat them!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l13-the-girl-who-ne: When Iryna was nine, she broke her leg in a car accident. The doctors were not sure that she could run again. For months she walked with crutches, and she felt very sad when she watched other children playing. Her grandfather had an idea. Every morning he took her to the swimming pool. In water her leg didn't hurt so much. At first she could swim only one length. After a month she could swim ten. A swimming coach noticed her. "You have good technique," he said. "Do you want to train with my group?" Iryna said yes immediately. Training was hard. She got up at six, swam before school and again in the evening. Sometimes she cried because she was tired. But she never gave up. At thirteen she won her first competition in the city. At fifteen she became a member of the national junior team. Last year, at seventeen, she won a silver medal at the European Championship. "People often ask me about my secret," Iryna says. "There is no secret. Every day you do a little more than yesterday. That's all."
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u5-l14-sport-through-t: Our class made a timeline of sport for the school corridor. Here are some of the facts we found. 776 BC: The first Olympic Games were held in ancient Greece. Only one event, a short running race, was organised. 1863: The first football rules were written in London. 1891: Basketball was invented by a teacher in the USA. 1896: The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens. 1900: Women competed in the Olympic Games for the first time. They played tennis and golf. 1924: The first Winter Olympic Games were organised in France. 1960: The first Paralympic Games were held in Rome. 1994: Ukraine took part in the Winter Olympics for the first time as an independent country. Figure skater Oksana Baiul won gold. Our timeline was hung on the wall next to the gym. Now students stop and read it every day. Last week somebody added a new fact with a pencil: "2026: 7-B won the school tug of war!"
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l1-a-hero-at-the-bu: Last winter Hlib, a 13-year-old from Rivne, became a local hero. Here is what happened. Hlib was waiting at a bus stop after school when an old man suddenly fell down on the ice. He hit his head and didn't move. There was a small wound on his forehead, and it was bleeding. Many people just looked. But Hlib reacted immediately. He remembered his first aid lessons at school. First, he checked if the man was breathing. He was. Then Hlib called 103 for an ambulance and explained where they were. While they were waiting, he put his scarf under the man's head and pressed a clean tissue on the wound to stop the bleeding. He talked to the man calmly and asked him not to move. The ambulance came in ten minutes. The doctor said that Hlib probably saved the man from a much worse situation. "In an emergency, the first minutes are the most important," she said. Later the man's family came to Hlib's school to thank him. "I just paid attention and didn't panic," Hlib said. "Everybody should learn first aid. It's not difficult, and it can save a life."
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l2-sports-injuries: Sport is good for you, but it can also be dangerous. Our school nurse, Mrs Hrytsai, told us about the most common sports injuries and how to avoid them. "The most common injury is a sprained ankle," she said. "It happens when you land badly after a jump. Basketball and volleyball players know it well. Your ankle becomes swollen and it hurts to walk." "Footballers often hurt their knees. Runners can get pain in their shins if they run too much on hard roads. And in winter many people break their wrists when they fall on the ice." "What should you do if you get hurt? Remember the word RICE: Rest, Ice, Compression and Elevation. Stop playing, put ice on the injury, wrap it with a bandage and lift your leg or arm up." "But the best thing is to avoid injuries. Always warm up before training. Wear the right shoes. Drink water. And listen to your body: if something hurts, stop!" Then she showed us some warm-up exercises. Everybody tried them, even our PE teacher.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l3-inside-your-body: Your body is an amazing machine. Every second, many organs work together to keep you alive. Your heart is a strong muscle about the size of your fist. It beats about 100,000 times a day and pumps blood all around your body. When you run, it beats faster. Your lungs are like two big sponges in your chest. When you breathe in, they fill with air. Oxygen from the air goes into your blood. When you breathe out, they push out carbon dioxide. Smoking damages the lungs, so they can't work well. Your tongue is not only for talking. It helps you to taste food: sweet, salty, sour and bitter. A doctor often asks you to show your tongue, because its colour can show if you are ill. Your brain is the boss of the whole body. It uses about one fifth of all your energy, even when you sleep. How can you help your body? Move every day, eat fruit and vegetables, drink water and sleep for eight or nine hours. Your heart and lungs will thank you!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l4-at-the-doctors: Ivanka, 13, didn't feel well for three days. She had a sore throat, a headache and a high temperature. Her mum made an appointment with the family doctor. Doctor: Good morning, Ivanka. What seems to be the problem? Ivanka: I've got a sore throat and a headache. And I feel very tired. Doctor: When did it start? Ivanka: On Monday. On Tuesday I had a temperature of 38.5. Doctor: Let me look at your throat. Say "Ah". Yes, it's red. Now I'll listen to your lungs. Breathe in... and out. Good, your lungs are clear. Mum: Is it a serious disease? Doctor: No, it's not serious. It's a throat infection. The symptoms are typical. I'll give you a prescription for some pills. Take one pill three times a day after meals. Drink a lot of warm tea with honey and stay in bed for a few days. Ivanka: Can I go to school? Doctor: Not this week. You need treatment and rest. Come back for a check-up on Friday. And remember: see your doctor regularly, not only when you are ill. On the way home Ivanka smiled. Three days without maths tests!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l5-if-you-feel-unwe: Our school nurse made a poster for the medical room. It has simple rules that are always true. If you cut your finger, you clean it and put on a plaster. If you have a nosebleed, you sit down and lean forward, not backwards. If you touch something very hot, you put your hand under cold water for ten minutes. If you get stung by a bee, you remove the sting and put something cold on it. If you don't drink enough water, you get a headache. If you sit at the computer for hours, your eyes get tired. If you eat too many sweets, your teeth go bad. If you feel dizzy, you sit down and tell an adult. At the bottom of the poster the nurse wrote: "If you don't know what to do, you come to the medical room!"
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l6-taking-medicine: Medicine can help us, but only if we use it correctly. Our biology teacher invited a pharmacist, Ms Romaniuk, to talk to our class. "Many medicines you can buy in a chemist's," she explained, "but some need a prescription. That means a doctor must prescribe them for you. Never take someone else's medicine, even your brother's or your mum's." "Always read the label. It tells you how much to take and how often. Some pills you take before meals, some after meals. If you take more than you should, it doesn't help faster. It can make you very ill." "Children should take medicine only when an adult gives it to them. And keep medicines away from little brothers and sisters. Some pills look like sweets!" Then a student asked a funny question: "Can medicine help my dog do tricks?" Everybody laughed. "No," Ms Romaniuk smiled, "but if your dog is ill, the vet can give it treatment too." At the end she gave us a small first-aid kit for our classroom.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l7-calling-the-scho: During the lunch break several students came to the medical room. Here is what the school nurse heard that day. "I've got a stomachache," said Vasyl from the fifth form. "I ate three pies very quickly." The nurse gave him some warm water and told him to eat slowly next time. "My eyes are red and itchy, and I keep sneezing," said Lilia, 12. "It happens every spring." "It sounds like an allergy to flowers," the nurse said. "Tell your parents and visit the doctor." "I've got a cough and a runny nose," said Bohdan, 13. The nurse checked his temperature. It was normal. "It's just a cold. Wash your hands often and drink warm drinks." "I hit my elbow on the door," said little Nastia from the first form, crying. The nurse put ice on it and gave her a sticker with a smiling bear. Nastia stopped crying immediately. At the end of the day the nurse wrote everything in her notebook. "Four students, four different problems," she said. "Every day is different here!"
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l8-a-terrible-morni: Last Monday was a terrible morning for Oksana, 13. Everything went wrong. When her alarm clock rang, she realised that she had forgotten to charge her phone. It was dead. When she got to the kitchen, her brother had already eaten all the cornflakes. She had only a piece of bread. When she ran out of the house, she saw that the bus had just left. She had to walk to school in the rain. When she arrived at school, the first lesson had already started. The teacher looked at her and said, "Good afternoon, Oksana!" Everybody laughed. At break she felt hot and dizzy. The school nurse checked her temperature: 38.2. "Oksana, you're ill," she said. "Have you had breakfast?" Oksana shook her head. When her mum came to take her home, Oksana felt terrible. But in the evening, after hot soup and a long sleep, she felt much better. "Mum," she said, "I think I had felt ill before I left the house. That's why everything went wrong!"
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l9-healthy-habits: Our class did a "healthy habits challenge" for one month. Each of us chose one new habit. Here are some results. Dmytro decided to go to bed before ten o'clock. "At first it was hard because I usually play games until late," he said. "But now I wake up without an alarm clock and I'm not tired in the first lesson." Iryna gave up fizzy drinks. She drinks water with lemon instead. "I feel more energy, and I've saved money too!" Kyrylo walked to school instead of taking the bus. It's two kilometres each way. "I've lost two kilos, and I see my friends on the way." Sofiia started eating breakfast every day. Before, she only had a cup of tea. "Now I don't feel hungry or dizzy at school." Andrii tried to use his phone less, only one hour a day. "That was the hardest," he admitted. "But I read two books this month!" At the end the class agreed: small habits make a big difference. Our teacher's habit? She stopped drinking five cups of coffee a day!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l10-what-happened-t: On Monday Roman came to school with his arm in a plaster cast. Everybody wanted to know what had happened. Olena: Roman! What happened to you? Roman: I broke my arm on Saturday. Olena: Oh no! How did it happen? Roman: I was skateboarding in the park. I was trying a new trick, and I fell off the board. Olena: Weren't you wearing a helmet? The doctor said I must wear the cast for five weeks. Olena: Five weeks! What about PE? Roman: No PE, no skateboarding, no basketball. And I can't write with my right hand. Olena: So who's going to do your homework? Roman: Hmm. I was hoping you could help me! Olena laughed and took a marker. "First, let me sign your cast," she said. k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l11-the-mountain-re: Last summer a group of six teenagers went hiking in the Carpathians with their teacher, Mr Fedorenko. On the second day something went wrong. They were walking down a steep path when Zakhar slipped on a wet stone. He fell and twisted his ankle badly. He couldn't stand on it. The group was far from any village, and there was no mobile signal. Mr Fedorenko stayed calm. He checked Zakhar's ankle, put a cold, wet cloth on it and wrapped it with a bandage from the first-aid kit. Two students, Maria and Ivan, walked up the hill to find a signal. After twenty minutes they called the mountain rescue service and told them the exact place from their map. Meanwhile, the others made a stretcher from two long sticks and a jacket. They carried Zakhar slowly down to a wider path. After two hours a rescue team arrived in a special car. They took Zakhar to the hospital. Luckily, his ankle wasn't broken, just sprained. "I was scared," Zakhar said later, "but my friends were amazing. I'm going back to the mountains next summer!"
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l12-health-myths: There are many things people say about health. Some are true, and some are myths. Let's check! "If you go out with wet hair, you catch a cold." Myth! Colds are caused by viruses, not by cold air. But you can feel uncomfortable and cold. "Carrots help you to see better." Partly true. Carrots have vitamin A, which is good for your eyes. But they won't help you see in the dark. "You should drink eight glasses of water a day." It depends. You get water from food and other drinks too. Drink when you are thirsty, and more when you do sport. "Reading in bad light damages your eyes." Myth! It makes your eyes tired, but it doesn't damage them. "An apple a day keeps the doctor away." Not exactly, but fruit is really good for you. Doctors say we should eat five portions of fruit and vegetables a day. "If you swallow chewing gum, it stays in your stomach for seven years." Myth! It goes out of your body in a few days, just like food. So next time your granny tells you something about health, smile and check it!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l13-a-letter-from-h: Dear class 7-A, Thank you so much for your cards and the big box of fruit! They made me really happy. As you know, I had an operation on my appendix last Tuesday. It started with a terrible pain in my stomach at night. My parents called an ambulance, and in the hospital the doctors said I needed an operation immediately. A surgeon operated on me the same night. I was asleep and didn't feel anything. Now I'm feeling much better. The doctors and nurses here are very kind. Every morning a nurse checks my temperature and gives me medicine. I can walk a little now, but I mustn't run or lift heavy things for a month. My roommate is a boy called Ostap. He broke his leg playing football. We play board games all day and tell each other jokes. The food is not like Mum's, but it's OK. I'm going home on Saturday, and I hope I'll be back at school in a week. Please tell Ms Bondarenko that I'm reading my English book! I miss you all. See you soon! Love, Marta
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l14-be-your-own-doc: Doctors say that most health problems can be prevented. Many of the most important things depend on you. Here is our class's "Be Your Own Doctor" guide. Sleep: Teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep. If you don't sleep enough, you can't concentrate and you get ill more often. Food: Eat breakfast every day. Choose fruit instead of crisps. Don't skip meals, and don't eat too late. Movement: Move for at least one hour a day. You don't need a gym. Walking, dancing and riding a bike are great. Screens: Take a break from your phone or computer every half an hour. Look out of the window to rest your eyes. Hygiene: Wash your hands before eating and after the toilet. Brush your teeth twice a day. Feelings: Health isn't only about the body. If you feel sad or worried for a long time, talk to someone you trust: a parent, a teacher or the school psychologist. And remember: if something is really wrong, don't be your own doctor. See a real one!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u6-l15-a-day-in-the-li: Natalia works as a paramedic on an ambulance in Lviv. We asked her to describe a typical day. "My shift starts at eight in the morning and lasts twelve hours. When I arrive, I check the ambulance: the medicines, the oxygen and all the equipment must be ready." "Every day is different. Today, by lunchtime, we had already been to four calls. First, an old woman had fallen in her kitchen. Then a man had a heart problem in a shop. After that, a boy had cut his hand badly on glass, and finally a woman needed help in the street because she felt dizzy." "The hardest part is the speed. You must decide very quickly. The best part is when people say thank you. Last month a little girl drew a picture of our ambulance for us. It's on the wall in our station." "Do I get tired? Yes, very. After a shift I sleep for ten hours. But I love my job. Every day I help somebody." "My advice to young people? Learn first aid. You don't need to be a paramedic to save a life."
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l1-tonight-at-the-c: Our town cinema has a new programme for the weekend. Here are four films. Which one would you choose? "The Silver Key" (adventure): Two teenagers find an old key in their grandmother's house. It opens a door to a strange world where a dark foe has put a spell on the people. The friends must solve three puzzles to break the spell and save the land. "Smooth Talker" (comedy): Max is a charming con artist who takes money from rich and greedy people. But one day he meets a clever little girl who sees through all his tricks. Soon she starts to change him. "Road Home" (drama): After a long time abroad, a young musician decides to hit the road and travel back to his village on an old motorbike.
