Nobody in society can be trusted, not even her partner. Tickets cost 150 hryvnias. Students get a 20% discount on Sundays. Don't forget the popcorn!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l2-what-kind-of-fil: We asked students in our school about their favourite film genres. Here are their answers. "I love animated films. People think they are only for children, but the best cartoons have deep stories and amazing music. I've watched some of them ten times!" Vira, 12 "I'm a fan of science fiction. I like films about space, robots and the future. They make me think about what the world will be like when I'm old." Matvii, 13 "Horror films? No, thank you! I prefer comedies. After a long school day I just want to laugh." Daryna, 13 "I like documentaries, especially about animals and nature. You can learn a lot from them, and the camera work is incredible." Oleksandr, 12 "My favourite are musicals. I sing along to every song, and my brother says I'm too loud!" Uliana, 13 "Historical films are the best for me. I like to see how people lived hundreds of years ago, what they wore and what they ate." Taras, 13 The survey showed that comedies and animated films are the most popular in our school. Horror films were the least popular.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l3-cinema-or-theatr: Our class went to the cinema in September and to the theatre in October. Then our teacher asked: which was better? In the cinema the lights went down and the huge screen lit up. We sat in soft red seats with popcorn and drinks. The sound was so loud that the seats shook during the action scenes. The film was exciting, but some people were looking at their phones. The theatre was completely different. It was an old building with three balconies decorated with gold. Our seats were on the first balcony, so we could see the whole stage. When the heavy red curtain went up, everybody was silent. The actors were real people, just a few metres from us. We could see their faces and hear their breath. At the end the audience stood up and clapped for five minutes. The actors came out and bowed again and again. In the class discussion most students chose the cinema because it's more modern and you can eat popcorn. But many said that the theatre was more magical. "In the cinema you watch a story," said Halyna. "In the theatre you're inside it."
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l4-theatres-of-the-: Some theatres are famous not only for their shows but also for their buildings. The Sydney Opera House in Australia looks like white sails on the water. Its design was a great renewal of theatre architecture. Inside there are several halls, and the biggest one has more than two thousand seats. The Shanghai Grand Theatre in China is made of glass and steel. At night it shines like a crystal box. Shows there are often in Chinese, but there are subtitles in English on a screen above the stage. The Lviv Opera House in Ukraine is one of the most beautiful in Europe. It has a grand staircase, a mirror hall and a painting on the main curtain. Many operas there are based on Ukrainian legends. The Globe Theatre in London is a copy of Shakespeare's theatre from 1599. It has no roof over the centre, so in the rain some of the audience get wet! Here you can see "Romeo and Juliet", a famous tragedy. When you enter any of these theatres, you find yourself in a different world, a space full of music, light and stories.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l5-our-puppet-theat: In our town there is a small puppet theatre, and it's my favourite place. I've been there more than twenty times since I was a little girl. The building is old and cosy. In the hall there are only a hundred seats, so every place is close to the stage. The walls are painted with characters from fairy tales: a fox, a wolf, a kind old man and a magic bird. Puppet shows are not only for little children. This year the theatre made a show for teenagers called "The Lost Voice". It's based on a Ukrainian legend about a girl who loses her voice and must find it in the forest. The puppets are as tall as people, and the actors move them in black clothes, so you almost don't see them. Last month our class visited the theatre backstage. A puppet maker showed us how she makes puppets from wood, paper and fabric. One puppet can take three weeks to make! Then we tried to move a puppet ourselves. It was much harder than it looks. The actors say that a good puppet has a soul. After that visit, I believe them. Name: Solomiia, 12

Dmytro "The best actor was definitely Mariana. She was incredibly good as the queen. She wasn't old enough for the role, but she acted like a real queen!" Oleh Our drama teacher read the reviews and smiled. "You're quite good critics," she said. "Next year you can write for a real newspaper!"
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l7-child-stars: Some actors become famous when they are still at school. Is it a dream or a difficult life? Ruslana, 14, from Dnipro, has played in three films and one TV series. She started acting when she was eight, after a casting at her school. "It's fun, but it's real work," she says. "Sometimes we film for ten hours a day. I do my homework between scenes." Ruslana has a tutor on set who helps her with school subjects. Her mum is always with her. "I miss my friends sometimes," she admits. "When they go to a birthday party, I'm often in another city filming." Many child stars have problems when they grow up. People only remember them as children, and it's hard to find new roles. Some stop acting and choose other jobs. But others become great actors. Some famous Hollywood stars started their careers as children and won important prizes as adults. Ruslana knows what she wants. "I want to study at a theatre university and play in a real theatre. Films are great, but nothing is better than a live audience."
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l8-film-types-quiz: How well do you know film types? Read the descriptions and guess. Type 1: The story happens in space or in the future. There are often robots, aliens and amazing technology. People ask: "What will the world be like?" Type 2: The main characters are drawn or made on a computer. Animals can talk, and anything is possible. Children and adults both love them. Type 3: There are a lot of songs and dances. The characters sing when they are happy, sad or in love. Type 4: There is a mystery, often a crime. A clever detective looks for clues and finally finds the criminal. Type 5: Heroes go on a dangerous journey. They climb mountains, cross rivers and fight enemies. Type 6: It tells true stories about real people, animals or places. There are no actors, just real life. Type 7: It's very scary. People in the cinema scream and hide behind their hands. Answers: 1 science fiction, 2 animated film, 3 musical, 4 detective film, 5 adventure film, 6 documentary, 7 horror film. How many did you get right?
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l9-bigger-better-th: Our class compared three films we watched in English lessons: an animated film, an adventure film and a documentary about whales. The adventure film was the longest. It lasted two hours and twenty minutes. The animated film was shorter, and the documentary was the shortest, only fifty minutes. Most students thought the animated film was funnier than the adventure film. But the adventure film was more exciting. The final battle was the most exciting scene of all three films. The documentary was not as exciting as the others, but it was the most interesting. We learned that a blue whale's heart is as big as a small car! The music in the animated film was better than in the adventure film. "It was the best music I've heard this year," said Anhelina. The special effects in the adventure film were the most expensive. But some students said the whales in the documentary were more beautiful than any computer effects. In the end we voted. The animated film won, the adventure film was second, and the documentary was third. "But the documentary taught us the most," our teacher said.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l10-cartoons-then-a: My grandpa says that cartoons were better in his childhood. I'm not so sure. So we watched an old Ukrainian cartoon and a new one together and compared them. The old cartoon was about Cossacks. It was drawn by hand, and the colours were simpler than in modern cartoons. But the characters were funnier and the jokes were cleverer than I expected. Grandpa laughed as loudly as I did. The new cartoon was made on a computer. The pictures were brighter and more detailed. The hero could fly, and the action scenes were much faster. It was the most colourful cartoon I've ever seen. "The new one is more beautiful," Grandpa admitted, "but the old one has more soul. The artists drew every picture by hand. That's the hardest way." I think the new cartoon was more exciting, but the old one was easier to understand. The music in the old cartoon was the best: we were both singing the song for the whole evening! In the end we agreed: a good story is the most important thing. Old or new, hand-drawn or computer-made, the best cartoons make people of all ages laugh together.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l11-movie-night: It's Friday evening. Four friends are at Nadiia's house, deciding what to watch. Nadiia: So, what shall we watch? Any ideas? Bohdan: What about an action film? k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l12-how-to-write-a-: Our teacher gave us a plan for writing a film review. Here it is, with an example by Yeva, 13. 1. Title and type: "Paddington in Peru" is a family comedy. k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l13-the-school-film: This spring our school had its first film festival. Students made short films, no longer than five minutes, with their phones. There were twelve films. The jury was made up of two teachers, a local journalist and a student from the eleventh form. The film "The Last Leaf" by 7-A won the prize for the best drama. The students filmed the river near the school every week for three months and showed how it changes. Our class, 7-B, made an animated film with plasticine figures. We didn't win, but we got a special prize for "the most creative idea". It took us 1,200 photos to make three minutes of film! The festival was such a success that it will happen every year now.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l14-behind-the-scen: When we watch a film, we see the actors. But hundreds of people work behind the scenes. Here are some of them. The director is the boss on set. He or she tells the actors how to play and decides how every scene should look. The screenwriter writes the script: the story and every word the actors say. The camera operator films the scenes. Sometimes the same short scene is filmed twenty times from different angles! The make-up artist can turn a young actor into an old man or a monster. For some fantasy films make-up takes four or five hours every morning. The costume designer makes the clothes. In historical films every button must be right for the time. The stunt person does the dangerous scenes instead of the actor: jumping from buildings, falling from horses or driving fast cars. The composer writes the music. Without music, even the most exciting scene can feel boring. At the end of every film there is a long list of names. Next time, don't leave the cinema immediately. Stay and read them: they are the people who made the magic.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l15-my-favourite-fi: Our English teacher asked us to write about our favourite film. Here is what Ihor, 13, wrote. "My favourite film is 'The Lion King'. I first watched it when I was five, and I've watched it many times since then. It's an animated film from 1994, but there is also a newer version made on a computer. The story takes place in Africa. A young lion, Simba, is the son of the king, Mufasa. His evil uncle Scar wants to be king. After a terrible event, Simba runs away and grows up far from home with two funny friends, Timon and Pumbaa. Finally, he must go back and fight for his land. I like this film because it's about growing up, family and being brave. The music is fantastic. I know all the songs by heart, and my little sister sings them too. The saddest scene is when Simba loses his father. The funniest characters are Timon and Pumbaa. Their song 'Hakuna Matata' means 'no worries'. I think 'The Lion King' is one of the best animated films ever. Everybody should see it at least once!"
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u7-l16-curtain-call: The school year is almost over, and our drama club is preparing its big summer show. This year it's a musical based on an old Ukrainian fairy tale about a clever girl and a greedy king. Rehearsals started three months ago. The actors practise twice a week, and in the last two weeks they have practised every day. The songs were written by our music teacher, and the costumes were made by students' parents. The art club is painting the stage. Last week they finished the forest scene, and now they're painting the king's castle. Our class is helping too. Some of us are working with the lights, some are selling tickets, and I'm in charge of the curtain. It's an important job: if I open the curtain too early, the audience will see the actors getting ready! The show is next Friday at six o'clock. Tickets cost 50 hryvnias, and all the money will go to the local children's hospital. I'm a bit nervous, but also excited. When the show is over and the actors come out for the curtain call, I'll be the person who makes it happen.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l1-four-countries-i: Many people confuse England with the United Kingdom. In fact, the UK is made up of four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Each one has its own capital and its own character. England is the biggest. Its capital, London, is famous for red double-decker buses, black taxis and the bobby, a friendly British police officer. Many English people still enjoy high tea in the afternoon, with sandwiches, scones and cakes. Scotland is famous for its rugged mountains, lakes called lochs and old castles. Its capital is Edinburgh, but the biggest city is Glasgow. The Scots invented golf, and there are hundreds of golf courses in the country. Wales has a beautiful coastline with high cliffs and sandy beaches. Its capital is Cardiff. The Welsh have their own language, and road signs are written in Welsh and English. Northern Ireland is the smallest. Its capital, Belfast, is the city where the Titanic was built. Near the coast you can see the Giant's Causeway, thousands of stone columns made by a volcano long ago. Four countries, four flags, but one kingdom!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l2-cities-of-the-wo: We asked teenagers from four cities to describe their home towns in a few sentences. "I live in Tokyo, one of the biggest cities in the world. More than thirty-seven million people live here! It's very clean and safe, and the trains are always on time. My favourite place is a quiet temple garden near my house." Haruto, 13 "My city, Rio de Janeiro, is famous for its beaches and the giant statue of Christ on a mountain. In February we have a huge carnival with music and dancing for five days." Beatriz, 12 "I'm from Kraków in Poland. It has a beautiful old market square and a castle on a hill. There's a legend about a dragon that lived under the castle!" Zuzanna, 13 "I live in Kharkiv, the second biggest city in Ukraine. We have a huge square, many universities and a beautiful park with a children's railway. People here are strong and friendly." Danylo, 13 Every city has its own story. What would you say about yours?
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l3-packing-for-a-tr: The Savchenko family is going on holiday to Montenegro next week. Everybody is packing. Dad has made a list. "Passports, tickets, money, a phone charger, sun cream and a first-aid kit," he reads. "Without passports we won't go anywhere!" Mum is packing light summer clothes, swimsuits and hats. She's also taking a small guidebook. "I want to visit the old town of Kotor and climb to the fortress," she says. Yaroslav, 13, is packing his snorkel and a waterproof camera. He wants to film fish in the sea. He's also taking a book for the plane. His sister Kira, 9, is trying to pack her big teddy bear, three dolls and her bike. "Kira, the bike isn't going!" Dad says. "And only one toy." After a long discussion, the teddy bear wins. Grandma is staying at home to look after the cat and the plants. "Send me lots of photos," she says, "and don't forget the sun cream!" On the morning of the trip everybody is excited. The taxi arrives at five. Dad checks the list one more time. Passports? Yes!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l4-famous-sights-ar: Every year millions of people travel to see famous sights. Here are some of the most popular. The London Eye is a giant Ferris wheel on the River Thames. From the top you can see the whole city. A ride takes about thirty minutes. The Taj Mahal in India is one of the most beautiful buildings in the world. It is a memorial, dedicated by an emperor to his wife after she died. Its white marble changes colour in the sunlight. The White House in Washington is the official residence and workplace of the president of the USA. It has 132 rooms and its own cinema. The Forbidden City in Beijing is a huge complex of palaces. Emperors lived there for almost five hundred years, and ordinary people couldn't enter. The Sagrada Família in Barcelona is a church that people have been building since 1882! Its architecture is unlike anything else, with towers that look like they are made of sand. St Sophia's Cathedral in Kyiv is more than a thousand years old. Inside you can see ancient mosaics and paintings on the walls. Which sight would you like to see first?
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l5-some-any-every-e: Our class went on a school trip to Chernivtsi. Here is a short report by Polina, 13. Every student brought a packed lunch, and some of us also brought snacks for the bus. The trip took five hours, so we needed a lot of snacks! In Chernivtsi we visited the university. It's a beautiful red-brick building, and each room is different. Some rooms have painted ceilings, and one hall looks like a palace. There weren't many tourists, so we could take a lot of photos. After that we walked along Olha Kobylianska Street. There are a few nice cafés there, and both of our teachers bought coffee. We had a little free time to buy souvenirs. I didn't have much money, but I bought some postcards and a magnet. In the evening all of us were tired, but nobody wanted to go home. "Can we come back next year?" somebody asked. The teachers smiled. "Maybe. Any ideas for next time?" "Lviv!" "Kamianets!" "The Carpathians!" Everybody had a different idea.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l6-a-walk-around-ky: Kyiv is one of the oldest cities in Europe. If you have only one day, here is a plan for a walk. Start in the morning at Independence Square, or Maidan. It's the main square of the country, where many important events took place. In the centre there is a tall white column with a statue on top. Then walk up to St Sophia's Cathedral, with its golden domes. Climb the bell tower for a great view of the city. Not far away is the Golden Gate, the old entrance to the city. It was rebuilt in the twentieth century, and inside there is a small museum. After lunch, walk down Andriivskyi Descent, a steep old street full of artists, souvenir shops and street musicians. In the afternoon, take a bus to the Pyrohiv Open-Air Museum. Here you can find out how people lived in Ukrainian villages a hundred years ago. There are old windmills, wooden churches and houses from every region. End your day by the Dnipro near the Mother Ukraine monument. It is one of the tallest statues in Europe. Watch the sunset over the river and the bridges. What a day!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l7-places-worth-vis: Ukraine has many places that are worth visiting. Our class made a list of our favourites. Lviv: The old city centre is like an open-air museum. You can drink hot chocolate in a café, visit the Opera House and climb the town hall tower. At Christmas the whole city smells of gingerbread. Kamianets-Podilskyi: Here there's a huge stone fortress on a rock above a river canyon. In summer there are knight festivals with battles and old music. The Carpathians: This is the place for hiking in summer and skiing in winter. You can climb Hoverla, the highest mountain in Ukraine, 2,061 metres high. Odesa: The city by the sea is famous for its Opera House, the famous Odesa Steps and its humour. People here love jokes! Uman: Sofiyivka Park is one of the most beautiful parks in Europe, with waterfalls, lakes, grottos and statues. It was a present from a man to his wife. Shatsk Lakes: In the north-west there are more than thirty lakes with clean blue water. It's perfect for swimming, fishing and cycling. Which place is on your list?
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l8-our-summer-trips: After the summer holidays our English teacher asked: "Where did you travel?" Here are some answers. "We went camping by the Desna river. We slept in a tent, cooked on a fire and swam every day. One night it rained so heavily that our tent got wet, but it was still fun." Sviatoslav, 13 "I visited my aunt in Prague. I walked across the famous Charles Bridge and saw the old astronomical clock. Every hour little figures come out of it!" Oleksandra, 12 "We had a cycling trip in the Carpathians with my dad. We rode about thirty kilometres a day. My legs hurt, but the views were amazing." Ivan, 13 "My family went to the seaside in Bulgaria. I learned to dive and saw a small octopus." Viktoriia, 13 "I didn't travel far. I stayed with my grandparents in a village near Poltava. I helped with the cows and read twelve books. It was a quiet but happy summer." Matvii, 12 Our teacher said that every journey, big or small, teaches us something.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l9-and-but-because-: Mykyta, 13, wrote a travel blog about his first trip abroad. "In July my family went to Italy. We flew to Rome because it was faster than going by bus. I was a bit scared on the plane, but the flight was smooth. Rome is beautiful, but it was extremely hot, so we went sightseeing early in the morning. We saw the Colosseum and threw coins into the Trevi Fountain. People say that if you throw a coin, you will come back to Rome. Although I don't usually like museums, the Vatican Museums were amazing. The ceilings were painted with incredible pictures, and I couldn't stop looking up. Then we took a train to Venice. There are no cars there, so people travel by boat. We wanted to take a gondola, but it was too expensive, so we took a water bus instead. I ate pizza or pasta every day. However, my favourite thing was Italian ice cream. I tried twelve flavours in ten days! I loved the trip, and I want to learn some Italian before we go again."
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l10-interview-with-: Olena Hrytsenko has visited sixty countries. Our school magazine interviewed her when she came to talk to our school. Reporter: When did you start travelling? Olena: When I was a student. I had very little money, so I travelled by train and slept in cheap hostels. Reporter: What was your most unusual trip? Olena: I spent a week with a family of reindeer herders in Norway. We lived in a tent, and it was minus thirty degrees! Reporter: Which country surprised you most? Olena: Japan. Everything is so polite and organised. Even the trains say "sorry" when they are one minute late. Reporter: Have you ever had problems on a trip? Olena: Of course. I once lost my passport in Peru. It took me two weeks to get a new one. But I made friends with the people at the embassy! Reporter: What is your advice for young travellers? Olena: Learn languages, be curious and respect local traditions. And always keep a copy of your passport. Reporter: Where are you going next? Olena: To Mongolia. I want to ride horses across the steppe.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l11-a-day-in-london: London is one of the most visited cities in the world. Here is a plan for a day there. Start at the Tower of London, a castle more than nine hundred years old. You can see the Crown Jewels and the famous ravens. People say that if the ravens leave, the kingdom will fall! Then walk across Tower Bridge, the beautiful bridge with two towers. Sometimes it opens to let big ships pass. Take a red double-decker bus to Trafalgar Square, with Nelson's Column and four huge lions. The National Gallery is right there, and it's free! Walk to Buckingham Palace, the King's residence in London. If you are lucky, you can see the Changing of the Guard, with soldiers in red jackets and tall black hats. In the afternoon, have a picnic in Hyde Park or go boating on the lake. In the evening, take a ride on the London Eye and watch the city lights. Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament are just across the river. London is expensive, but many of its museums are free. And remember: in London, cars drive on the left!
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l12-at-the-tourist-: Dariia and her mum are on holiday in Edinburgh. They go to the tourist office in the morning. Assistant: Good morning! How can I help you? Mum: Hello. We're here for three days. What can we see? Assistant: You must visit Edinburgh Castle. It's on a rock in the centre of the city. Here's a map. Tickets are 20 pounds for adults and 12 for children. Dariia: Are there any guided tours? Assistant: Yes. A tour guide takes groups around the castle every hour. And in the evening there's a ghost tour in the old town. It's very popular with teenagers! Dariia: A ghost tour? Cool! Mum: What about museums? Assistant: The National Museum of Scotland is free. There's also a cathedral on the Royal Mile and a beautiful bridge over the Firth of Forth. You can go there on an excursion by bus. Mum: Do we need to book the excursion? Assistant: Yes, it's better to book a day before. I can do it for you now. Mum: Great. And we're from Ukraine. Do we need a visa for a day trip to the Highlands? Assistant: No, the Highlands are still in Scotland. No visa needed! Everybody laughed.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l13-around-the-worl: In 1873 the French writer Jules Verne wrote a famous novel, "Around the World in Eighty Days". Its hero, an English gentleman called Phileas Fogg, makes a bet with his friends. He says he can travel around the whole world in just eighty days. Fogg leaves London with his servant, Passepartout. They travel by train and ship across Europe to Egypt, and then to India. In India there is no railway in one part, so they ride an elephant through the jungle! They continue to Hong Kong, Japan and across the Pacific Ocean to San Francisco. Then they cross America by train. On the way the train is attacked, and Passepartout bravely saves the passengers. At last they sail across the Atlantic to Britain. When Fogg arrives in London, he thinks he is one day late and has lost the bet. But then he realises that, because he travelled east, he has gained a day. He runs to his club just in time and wins! Today you can fly around the world in less than two days. But Fogg's journey shows that travel is about adventures and the people you meet, not only about speed.
k6aud/_final_k7t2|u8-l14-postcards-from-: At the end of the school year our English teacher asked us to write imaginary postcards from places we studied. Here are three of them. Dear Mum and Dad, I'm in Scotland! Today I climbed to Edinburgh Castle, and the view was amazing. Tomorrow we're going on a boat trip on Loch Ness. I hope to see the monster! Love, Kira Hi Danylo, Greetings from Tokyo! The city is huge and very clean. I've eaten sushi every day, and I tried to read the signs, but it's impossible. Yesterday I saw a robot that serves coffee! See you soon, Maks Dear Grandma, I'm writing from Kamianets-Podilskyi. The fortress is like a castle from a fairy tale. There was a knight festival, and a real knight let me hold his sword. It was very heavy! I've bought you a little clay jug as a present. Kisses, Vira Our teacher put all the postcards on a big map on the classroom wall. Now the map is full of colourful cards from all over the world. "Next year," she said, "I hope you will send me real postcards!"
